design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of existing laboratory records, filed as cross-sectional because each sample was analysed once: cannabinoid and terpene results for 89,923 dried-flower samples that licensed cultivators submitted for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in Alaska, Oregon, Washington, Florida, Michigan and California (December 2013 to January 2021), shared through the data-sharing programme of Leafly, a consumer cannabis website. Each sample's producer-given name was matched to Leafly's strain database, which supplied a popular strain name and the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category associated with that name. The study maps chemical types (THC:CBD ratio classes; three terpene clusters by k-means) and tests how well the categories and the strain names track terpene profiles (silhouette scores; cosine similarity against randomly shuffled names; over-representation in clusters). No people were studied and no effects were measured.
can_establish: How cannabinoid and terpene content varied across nearly 90,000 compliance-tested flower samples from six US states, and how weakly the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category linked to each strain name (and, less weakly, the strain names themselves) tracked terpene profiles in THC-dominant flower.
cannot_establish: Whether labels or chemical types predict how a product feels (no effects were measured); whether the label printed on a package matches its chemistry (categories came from one website's database by name matching); whether THC or CBD content differs by category (not analysed); or whether differences between states reflect the plants or the six laboratories' different methods (the authors say they cannot tell).

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people. Records of flower samples that licensed cultivators submitted for state-mandated compliance testing before sale to licensed retailers. Six testing laboratories (CannTest, Alaska; ChemHistory, Oregon; Confidence Analytics, Washington; Modern Canna Science, Florida; PSI Labs, Michigan; SC Labs, California) consented to share their complete data for a period within December 2013 to January 2021; the data came through Leafly's data-sharing programme for university-affiliated researchers (p. 4; pp. 21–23; Tables 1–3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Dried female flower only; products made from flower (pre-rolls, edibles, concentrates) excluded (p. 22). Removed: 11 duplicate rows, 80 samples with any single cannabinoid above 40% by weight, 2 with summed cannabinoids above 50%, and 591 with missing or zero values for both total THC and total CBD, given as 684 in all (p. 23). Terpene data removed for 4,234 samples (variance below 0.001, any terpene above 5%, or more than 10 zeros among the 14 common terpenes) (p. 24). Main analyses used only compounds measured by every laboratory: six cannabinoids and 14 terpenes or terpene groups (pp. 24–25).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (no people). Cannabinoid samples by laboratory after cleaning: Washington 53,190, Oregon 13,508, California 8,112, Michigan 7,240, Alaska 6,253, Florida 1,620; terpene samples: Oregon 11,720, Washington 11,070, California 7,917, Alaska 6,173, Michigan 5,268, Florida 695; cultivators per laboratory from 5 (Florida) to 1,058 (California) (Table 3, p. 24).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 47.6% of cleaned samples had terpene data, because terpene testing is generally not legally required (p. 24). Of the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene data, 12,322 (29.9%) had no Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (Fig 6A legend, p. 11; Fig 7B, p. 13).
sample.selection_effects: What cultivators submitted for compliance testing at six laboratories that agreed to share data, not a random sample of what is sold; one producer can submit the same product many times, and the sample-level analyses count each submission. Washington supplies 59% of cannabinoid samples but 26% of terpene samples (editors' calculation from Table 3), so the cannabinoid and terpene analyses rest on different mixes of states. The terpene subset depends on which samples had optional terpene testing. The Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category is the one a consumer website attaches to a strain name, not what was printed on each package, and only names that matched the database could be labelled (81.5% of samples matched a strain name and 73.4% also a category, p. 23). The strain-name analysis was limited to the 41 names with at least five producers each submitting at least five samples (p. 27).

exposure.measurement: Two things were compared. Labels: strain names and Indica/Hybrid/Sativa categories from Leafly's strain database, matched to producer-given sample names by a string-matching algorithm supplemented with an expert dictionary of common name variants (pp. 22–23). Chemistry: each laboratory's own results, cannabinoids by HPLC with diode-array or UV detection and terpenes by gas chromatography with flame-ionization or mass-spectrometry detection, converted to % by weight; total THC computed as 0.877 × THCA + THC, with analogous formulas for other cannabinoids (Table 1, p. 22; p. 24).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (product chemistry; no human exposure).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (no people studied). The analogous limitation: compounds measured by only some laboratories were left out of the main analyses, and the authors note that one of them could be an important chemical marker (p. 21).

comparison.controls: No control group. Category groups were compared with each other and with two groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's dominant terpene; three k-means clusters); strain-name consistency was compared with a baseline made by shuffling names at random across producers, repeated 200 times (pp. 10–14; pp. 27–28).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to people. Unmeasured sample features: genotype, growing and storage conditions, and each laboratory's calibration; the authors cannot separate genetic from environmental or laboratory influences (p. 3; pp. 16–17; p. 21).

outcomes.instruments: Silhouette coefficient for each sample: how much closer its terpene profile (as % of the 14 measured terpenes) lies to its own label group than to the nearest other group, from −1 to 1, averaged over all 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene data. Cosine similarity of product-averaged terpene profiles among products sharing a strain name, against the shuffled baseline. Share of a name's products in its most common k-means cluster, against shuffling. Chi-square tests of category shares within each cluster against the overall shares. Welch's t-tests with an unequal-variance Cohen's d (d′), Spearman correlations, and PCA and UMAP plots for display (pp. 25–28).
outcomes.validity_norms: Silhouette and cosine similarity are standard clustering measures, but the paper sets no threshold for a label that 'works'. The k-means clusters and dominant-terpene groups are built from the same terpene data, so they score better than any outside label by construction; the informative quantity is the categories' own score near zero.
outcomes.operationalization: A label is taken to carry chemical information if samples sharing it have terpene profiles closer to each other than to samples with other labels. Only terpene profiles were used, and only in THC-dominant samples; THC and CBD content by category was not compared.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni within each family of tests: 3 comparisons of labelling systems, 41 strain-name consistency tests, 41 over-representation tests and 3 cluster chi-square tests (88 label-related tests, editors' count), plus 91 terpene pairs and smaller families elsewhere. With tens of thousands of samples nearly every comparison is significant, so the authors report d′ beside p (p. 25).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (automated analysis of laboratory records).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean silhouette scores in THC-dominant samples with terpene data: Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category −0.03; dominant terpene 0.27; k-means clusters 0.38 (Fig 6B, 6D, 6F, p. 11). Differences between labelling systems: k-means vs category |d′| = 3.49; dominant terpene vs category |d′| = 1.83; k-means vs dominant terpene |d′| = 0.54 (Fig 7A, p. 13; p. 12). Terpene diversity: THC-dominant products more diverse than balanced (|d′| = 0.74) and CBD-dominant products (|d′| = 0.89) (p. 10). Strain names more consistent than shuffled names for the majority of names, |d′| = 1.44 as printed (p. 14). Purple Punch: 96% of products in Cluster I vs 61.8% expected under shuffling, |d′| = 2.47 (p. 14). Dogwalker OG 100% in Cluster I (|d′| = 1110.4), Blue Dream 88.5% in Cluster II (|d′| = 1.2), Dutch Treat 85.9% in Cluster III (|d′| = 1.0) (p. 16). Cluster III total CBG median 0.98% vs 0.65% in the other clusters, |d′| = 0.57 (p. 12). Category shares by cluster (products): Sativa 30.9% and Indica 13.3% in Cluster III against 15.0% and 24.4% overall, χ² = 22.2 (Fig 9B, p. 17; p. 16). No confidence intervals are given for any estimate.
analysis.covariates: None. Data from the six laboratories were pooled, and laboratory or state was not adjusted for in the label analyses; the authors report similar clusters within each state in supplementary figures (S6), which were not in the PDF and were not read.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned. The cleaned dataset and code are stated to be public on GitHub; raw data are available on request with each laboratory's consent (Data Availability Statement, pp. 1–2; p. 24).
analysis.selective_reporting: THC and CBD content by Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category is not reported. Silhouette means appear only in the figures. The 'None' group (samples without a category) is included in the category silhouette analysis, and no score for the three categories alone is given. The text says Fig 7 shows THC, CBD and CBG distributions per cluster, which it does not.
analysis.power: Not a constraint for detecting differences: the sample is so large that negligible differences are significant, and the effect sizes rather than the p-values carry the information. The strain-name analyses rest on product averages for 41 names.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In THC-dominant flower, 96.5% of samples, terpene profiles barely separated by the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category tied to each strain name (mean silhouette −0.03, most samples negative), while the same samples grouped into three terpene types (caryophyllene–limonene 53%, myrcene–pinene 34%, terpinolene–myrcene 13%). Products sold under the same strain name by different producers were more alike than randomly assigned names for about two-thirds of the 41 names that at least five producers each sold with at least five samples, but consistency varied widely (Purple Punch 96% in one cluster, Tangie 62.5%), and two names were less consistent than chance. Sativa-categorized products were over-represented in the terpinolene-rich cluster (31% vs 15% overall), though most products there were still categorized Hybrid (56%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's statement that labels do not consistently align with the chemistry, while certain labels show a biased association, matches the results (p. 1). The discussion goes further: it calls marketing of Indica as sedating and Sativa as energizing "specious" (p. 19), says the category system is highly unlikely to indicate systematically different effects (p. 19), and calls label-based marketing deceptive (p. 21). No effects were measured; the step from chemistry to effects assumes that effects follow the measured chemistry, which the authors themselves describe as unconfirmed (p. 3; p. 20). The categories tested were a database's category for each strain name, not what was on each package, and THC or CBD content by category was not examined. The one positive association of a category with a cluster rests on a chi-square that appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts.

timeline.event: Two popular Dutch coffee-shop cultivars, one described as Sativa-dominant and one as Indica-dominant, differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but not in THC; 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other chemically

California cannabinoid and terpene data: limited differences between Indica and Sativa labels, some strain names more consistent than others (Elzinga et al., 2015, as described by Smith et al., p. 4).
Dutch flower samples: specific terpenes more often found in Indica- than in Sativa-labelled samples (Hazekamp et al., 2016, as described by Smith et al., p. 4).
Washington state data limited to total THC and CBD: no differences between Indica and Sativa labels (Jikomes & Zoorob, 2018, as described by Smith et al., p. 4).
US cannabinoid data: no clear relation between strain name and chemical type; terpenes not measured (Vergara et al., 2020, as described by Smith et al., p. 4).
This study: the largest dataset, six states, terpenes included; categories track terpene profiles poorly and strain names moderately.

replication.where_it_stands: Earlier, smaller single-region studies, as the authors summarize them, point the same way, and one Dutch study found some terpene differences by label, which echoes this study's terpinolene–Sativa skew. None of them, as described, recorded the label printed on retail packages or linked chemistry to measured effects; whether chemical types (rather than labels) predict effects remains untested in this literature.

funding.funder: No external funding stated. Leafly allowed N.J. to use some professional time to oversee the project and work on the manuscript but provided no other funding; the paper states that Leafly had no role in study design, laboratory data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Funding statement, p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: D.V. is founder and president of the non-profit Agricultural Genomics Foundation and sole owner of CGRI, LLC. N.J. is employed by Leafly Holdings, Inc., which allowed him professional time for the project (Competing interests, p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: The corresponding author is a Leafly employee and, by the author-contribution statement, conceived, supervised and validated the study (p. 28); Leafly's consumer strain database supplied the strain names, categories and popularity measures, and the laboratory data came through Leafly's data-sharing programme (p. 21). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Buy products at retail in several markets, record the strain name and Indica/Hybrid/Sativa label printed on each package, measure cannabinoids and terpenes in one laboratory with one validated method, and test in a blinded, randomized crossover study of people who use cannabis whether products matched for THC but differing in label or terpene type produce different effects.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Compliance-testing records fit the question of what licensed producers sent to market in these six states in 2013–2021; they are not retail purchases, and categories come from a database rather than from packaging.

Each laboratory's complete data for its period were used, but laboratories joined through a data-sharing programme (how many were approached is not stated), and the terpene subset depends on optional testing.
89,923 samples, 42,843 with terpene data, 41,201 THC-dominant samples in the label analysis.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Laboratories, states, methods and counts are given; each laboratory's period and the number of samples per producer are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Terpene analyses cover 47.6% of samples; 29.9% of THC-dominant samples with terpene data had no category and were analysed as a 'None' group.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: HPLC and gas chromatography are standard, but detectors, units and terpene panels differ by laboratory, and the label is a database category matched by name.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Six laboratories with unstandardized methods and no reported inter-laboratory calibration; the authors cannot tell laboratory differences from regional ones (p. 4; pp. 16–17).

Effect sizes and Bonferroni correction are used, but the cluster chi-square appears to have been computed on percentages, one d′ (1110.4) is a zero-variance artefact, repeat submissions are treated as independent in sample-level analyses, and no intervals are given.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents; laboratory participation is covered under item 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI prevalence checklist fits a descriptive cross-sectional analysis of product records; no instrument is designed for label-validity analyses of product chemistry. The central finding, that the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category tied to strain names does not separate terpene profiles, rests on a very large sample, is visible in the scatter of Fig 6A, and is unlikely to be reversed by the problems listed: unstandardized laboratory methods add noise that could blur groups, yet they did not blur the data-derived clusters or the stronger strain-name consistency. The positive associations (specific names, the Sativa–terpinolene skew) and all comparisons between states are less secure. Citable for labels against terpene chemistry in compliance-tested US flower, 2013–2021; not for effects, for package labels, or for THC content by category.

key_findings.finding: The dataset: 89,923 dried-flower samples after cleaning, from six compliance-testing laboratories in six US states (Alaska, Oregon, Washington, Florida, Michigan, California), tested between December 2013 and January 2021; 42,843 (47.6%) had terpene data; 3,319 cultivators and 3,087 cultivar names.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data collection, 6th paragraph (p. 23); Data processing › Raw data filtering and outlier removal, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 24)

key_findings.finding: 96.5% of samples were THC-dominant (THC:CBD of 5:1 or more; n = 86,740), 2.2% balanced (n = 1,940) and 1.4% CBD-dominant (1:5 or less; n = 1,243) in the pooled data; THC-dominant samples were also the majority in each state (S2 Fig, not in the PDF). [The paper gives the percentages for the aggregate only; per state it says only that most samples were THC-dominant (p. 4). Fig 1 counts confirmed at 300 dpi.]
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabinoid composition of U.S. commercial Cannabis, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Fig 1B–C legends (p. 5); Materials and methods › THC:CBD chemotypes (p. 24)
key_findings.note: The counts are printed only inside the Fig 1 panels (image text, read on the rendered page); they reproduce the percentages (86,740 of 89,923 = 96.5%).

key_findings.finding: 3.9% of samples had total CBD and 23.1% total CBG of 1% by weight or more; in a PCA of six cannabinoids the first component explained 96% of the variance (tracking the THC:CBD ratio, rs = −0.51) and the second 3.6% (tracking CBG, rs = 0.95).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabinoid composition of U.S. commercial Cannabis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 84.5% of CBD-dominant samples had total THC above 0.3%, the threshold that legally defines hemp in the US; in CBD-dominant samples total THC and CBD were correlated (rs = 0.64).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabinoid composition of U.S. commercial Cannabis, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 4, continues p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Myrcene, β-caryophyllene and limonene were present at the highest levels; single terpenes rarely exceeded 0.5% by weight and most were below 0.2% in most samples; total terpene content averaged 2% by weight and correlated modestly with total cannabinoid content (rs = 0.37).
key_findings.locator: Results › Terpene composition of U.S. commercial Cannabis, 1st paragraph (begins p. 6, continues p. 7); Fig 3A (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: In 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene data, samples categorized Indica, Hybrid or Sativa were intermingled in terpene space: the mean silhouette score for the categories was −0.03 and most samples scored below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters (k-means vs categories |d′| = 3.49; dominant terpene vs categories |d′| = 1.83).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cluster analysis reveals distinct terpene chemotypes and poor validity of common commercial labels, 2nd paragraph (p. 10) and 4th paragraph (p. 12); Fig 6A–F (p. 11); Fig 7A (p. 13)
key_findings.note: Mean silhouette values are printed only inside Fig 6, and |d′| = 1.83 only inside Fig 7A (image text, read on 300-dpi crops). The category analysis includes a 'None' group of 12,322 samples (29.9%) without a category, beside Hybrid 17,616 (42.8%), Indica 6,681 (16.2%) and Sativa 4,582 (11.1%) (Fig 6A legend; Fig 7B); no score for the three categories alone is reported.

key_findings.finding: THC-dominant samples fell into three terpene clusters: Cluster I, high caryophyllene–limonene, 21,811 samples (52.9%); Cluster II, high myrcene–pinene, 14,188 (34.4%); Cluster III, high terpinolene–myrcene, 5,202 (12.6%); 87.4% of THC-dominant samples were in Clusters I or II. Cluster III had somewhat higher total CBG (median 0.98% vs 0.65%, |d′| = 0.57).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cluster analysis…, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 12); Fig 6E legend (p. 11); Fig 7B (p. 13); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 18)
key_findings.note: Cluster counts and percentages are printed only inside the Fig 6E legend and Fig 7B (image text, read on 300-dpi crops); 87.4% is in the Discussion text and equals (21,811 + 14,188) / 41,201.

key_findings.finding: Category shares by terpene cluster, among 13,401 THC-dominant products (12,063 with a category): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III (terpinolene-rich) Sativa 30.9%, Indica 13.3%, Hybrid 55.8%; Cluster I Sativa 11.1%, Indica 24.8%, Hybrid 64.1%; Cluster II Sativa 15.6%, Indica 27.4%, Hybrid 57.1%. Only Cluster III was reported as differing significantly from the overall shares (χ² = 22.2, P < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Some commercial labels are overrepresented in specific chemically defined clusters, 3rd paragraph (p. 16); Fig 9A legend and Fig 9B (p. 17)
key_findings.note: The percentages are printed only inside Fig 9B and the counts inside the Fig 9A legend (image text, read on a 300-dpi crop); product totals are the editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend (Hybrid 7,306, Indica 2,944, Sativa 1,813, None 1,338). Editors' calculation: a chi-square computed on the printed percentages instead of counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III, 1.2 for Cluster I and 0.6 for Cluster II, so the reported test appears to have used percentages (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Strain names: 41 names were attached to at least five producers with at least five samples each; the number of products per name correlated with the name's popularity on the website (rs = 0.59). For the majority of names, products from different producers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random (P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed), but consistency varied widely between names.
key_findings.locator: Results › Commercial "strain names" display differential levels of chemical consistency, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig 8A and 8C (p. 15); Materials and methods, Fig 8 paragraph (p. 27)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from the significance marks in Fig 8C (300-dpi crop): 26 of 41 names more consistent than the shuffled baseline, 13 not different, and 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) significantly less consistent. The shuffled baseline sits at a cosine similarity of about 0.69 (read from the figure), so even randomly paired products were fairly similar.

key_findings.finding: Purple Punch was the example of a consistent name (96% of its products in Cluster I, against 61.8% expected if names were shuffled; |d′| = 2.47) and Tangie of an inconsistent one (only 62.5% of its products in any single cluster). The most cluster-specific names were Dogwalker OG (100% in Cluster I), Blue Dream (88.5% in Cluster II) and Dutch Treat (85.9% in Cluster III); the authors note that even these are not perfectly tied to one chemical type and vary within their cluster.
key_findings.locator: Results › Commercial "strain names"…, 4th paragraph (p. 14); Some commercial labels are overrepresented…, 1st paragraph (begins p. 14, continues p. 16) and 2nd paragraph (p. 16); Fig 9D (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: The Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category was not read from packaging: Leafly's database supplied a popular strain name and the category associated with that name, matched to each sample's producer-given name by string matching plus an expert dictionary; 81.5% of samples matched a strain name and 73.4% also a category, the rest being labelled unknown.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data collection, 5th paragraph (begins p. 22, continues p. 23)

key_findings.finding: The authors state they cannot tell whether regional differences reflect true variation or measurement differences between laboratories, whose methods may not be standardized, and list as caveats the pooling of laboratory data, the absence of genotype and growing conditions, compounds not measured in every region, differing state regulations and the exclusion of hemp.
key_findings.locator: unchanged (the page field omits p. 4, which the locator cites, and the Discussion 2nd paragraph runs to p. 18)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa system does not reliably distinguish samples by chemical content, that it is highly unlikely to be a reliable indicator of systematically different effects, and that strain names may be better markers of chemistry than the categories but are far from ideal. [Source: 'may be a better marker', p. 19.]

reporting_issues.issue: The sample-cleaning figures do not add up. The text says 684 samples (0.75% of the raw dataset) were dropped, including 591 without THC or CBD values; Table 2 gives 90,016 samples before cleaning and Table 3 gives 89,923 after. By the editors' calculation the tables differ by 93 (equal to the 11 duplicates, 80 samples above 40% and 2 above 50%), 684 is 0.76% of 90,016, and 0.75% fits a raw total of about 90,600. The text also gives 3,087 unique cultivar names before cleaning, while Table 2 gives 3,090 (3,087 is the after-cleaning figure in Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the findings (under 1% of samples), but the size of the raw dataset and the point at which the 591 samples were removed are unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-square for Indica/Hybrid/Sativa shares within clusters appears to have been computed on percentages rather than product counts: using the printed percentages of Fig 9B as if they were counts reproduces the reported χ² of 22.2 for Cluster III (editors' calculation: 22.3) and gives 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, matching their reported non-significance. Product counts per cluster are not reported, so the tests cannot be redone.
reporting_issues.consequence: A chi-square on counts would be larger by a factor of the cluster's product count divided by 100; with thousands of products per cluster, the smaller differences in Clusters I and II (for example Sativa 11.1% vs 15.0%) would probably also reach significance. The direction of the Cluster III finding holds; the statement that Clusters I and II did not differ is not supported.

reporting_issues.issue: The effect size printed for Dogwalker OG (|d′| = 1110.4), beside 1.2 for Blue Dream and 1.0 for Dutch Treat, arises when all of a name's products fall in one cluster, leaving almost no variance in the denominator. The over-representation tests compare one name's proportion with a bootstrap distribution of shuffled averages by Welch's t-test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The d′ values for over-representation are not comparable across names and should not be cited as effect sizes; the percentages themselves are the usable result.

reporting_issues.issue: A single test result (P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44) is given for the statement that most strain names were more consistent than shuffled names, while the methods describe 41 separate tests; what the single statistic compares is not explained, and the number of names above chance is not stated in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count has to be read from the significance marks in Fig 8C (editors' count: 26 above, 13 not different, 2 below).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Fig 7C–7F shows the total THC, CBD and CBG distributions of each cluster, and the discussion says the clusters have similar total THC distributions (Fig 7), but Fig 7 contains only silhouette violins, stacked bars, a UMAP plot and terpene polar plots. The same paragraph cites 'Fig 4B–4D' for the cluster terpene profiles, which are in Fig 7D–7F.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that THC content was similar across the three terpene clusters is not backed by any value in the paper, apart from the CBG medians.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig 1A gives CBD values for 47,205 of the 89,923 samples (N printed under the CBD violin, image text); the paper does not say how samples without a CBD value were assigned a THC:CBD class, although the histogram has a separate 'infinite' bar for samples with zero THC or CBD (Fig 1C legend). The denominator of the 3.9% with CBD of 1% or more is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The THC-dominant share may include samples whose CBD was not measured; probably a small effect on the share of high-CBD samples, but not quantified.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the poor validity of the Indica/Sativa system agrees with other studies cites a single reference (ref. 71) whose title concerns repetitive genomic content in Cannabis; the earlier label studies are cited in the introduction (refs. 34, 46, 48, 49).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the earlier label studies, not ref. 71, are the relevant comparison (the cited paper was not read).
